title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.3 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
intro: After this lesson you can check the conditions for a one-sample $z$ interval, build the interval with $z^*$ and the standard error, work backwards from an interval, and write the conclusion in context.

moments.title: Confidence interval
moments.text: An interval estimate for a parameter, built around the sample proportion. The procedure is a one-sample $z$ interval for a population proportion.

moments.title: Define the parameter first
moments.text: Name the proportion, the response variable and the population in context.

moments.title: Ohio teens in marching band
moments.text: The goal is the proportion of all Ohio teens in a marching band, using a sample of 380.

moments.title: The middle 95%
moments.text: 95% of sample proportions fall within 1.96 standard deviations of $p$.

moments.title: Find $z^*$ in Desmos
moments.text: Normal with mean 0 and SD 1, Cumulative Probability, switch to bounds, inner, then enter the confidence level.

moments.title: The interval is a net
moments.text: Go 1.96 standard deviations each way from $\hat p$. If $\hat p$ is in the middle 95%, the net catches $p$.

moments.title: Why the net sometimes misses
moments.text: 5% of sample proportions fall outside the middle 95%, so some intervals miss $p$.

moments.title: Standard error
moments.text: We do not know $p$, so the standard error uses $\hat p$ in place of $p$ to estimate the standard deviation.

moments.title: Other confidence levels
moments.text: $z^*$ is 1.645 for 90% and 2.576 for 99%. More confidence needs a wider net.

moments.title: Margin of error
moments.text: The part you add and subtract, $z^*\times\text{SE}$. The interval is two margins wide.

moments.title: Marching band interval
moments.text: $\hat p=91/380\approx0.239$. With 95% confidence the interval runs from about 19.6% to 28.2%.

moments.title: Online homework platform
moments.text: 156 of 240 students support the switch. Build a 92% interval.

moments.title: Appropriateness conditions
moments.text: Random sample, $n$ at most 10% of the population, and at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

moments.title: Interval in Desmos
moments.text: Plus, Inference, $z$ test for proportions, enter successes and sample size, create, then open the confidence interval.

moments.title: Three parts of the conclusion
moments.text: State the confidence level, the interval, and the parameter in context.

moments.title: Work backwards from an interval
moments.text: Given 90% confidence and (0.42, 0.54), find $\hat p$, the margin of error, and $n$.

moments.title: Solve the margin of error for $n$

cards.name: Random
cards.text: The data come from a random sample.

cards.name: 10% condition
cards.text: $n$ is at most 10% of the population, so independence is reasonable.

cards.name: Large counts
cards.text: At least 10 successes and 10 failures in the sample: $n\hat p\ge10$ and $n(1-\hat p)\ge10$.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: In a confidence interval the large counts check uses the sample counts, $n\hat p$ and $n(1-\hat p)$, because $p$ is unknown. In a test (topic 3.5) you will use the null value instead.

sections.title: Build and report an interval with PANIC

questions.obj: Build and report a one-sample z interval with PANIC
questions.q: A random sample of 380 teenagers in Ohio finds that 91 are in the marching band. Construct and interpret a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all Ohio teenagers who are in the marching band.

steps.t: Parameter and Name: define $p$ and name the interval.

work.text: This is a one-sample $z$ interval for $p$, where $p$ is the proportion of all Ohio teenagers who are in the marching band.

steps.t: Assumptions: check random, 10%, and at least 10 successes and failures.

work.text: The sample is random. Assume Ohio has more than 3,800 teenagers, so 380 is less than 10% of them. Both counts are at least 10.

steps.t: Interval: find the point estimate, the critical value, and the standard error.

work.text: The standard error uses $\hat p$, because $p$ is unknown. $z^*=1.96$ is the critical value for the middle 95% of the standard normal distribution.

steps.t: Interval: find the margin of error and the interval.

work.text: The margin of error is how far to go above and below the point estimate.

steps.t: Conclusion: state the confidence level, the interval, and the parameter in context.

work.text: Use the exact interval endpoints and name the population and the variable.

questions.answer: I am 95% confident that the proportion of all Ohio teenagers who are in the marching band is between 0.1966 and 0.2824.

sections.title: Interval capture explorer
sections.intro: Each press draws 100 random samples and builds an interval from each one. Gray intervals catch the true $p$ and red intervals miss. Change the confidence level or the sample size and watch the widths and the capture rate.

stories.band: Suppose 24% of all Ohio teens are in a marching band. Each sample is 380 randomly chosen teens, and each one gives its own interval for $p$.
stories.big: Same population, but each sample is 1,500 teens. The intervals are much narrower.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Work through each task in it yourself, the way you would on the exam, then check what you observe.

steps.title: Find a critical value
steps.suppose: we want $z^*$ for a 92% confidence interval.
steps.observe: The two bounds are the same size with opposite signs, because the middle 92% is symmetric. Try 0.95 and 0.99 to see $z^*$ grow.
do: Keep [[Normal distribution]]. Enter 0 for mean and 1 for stdev, then press [[Create Distribution]].
Open [[Cumulative Probability]] and, under COMPUTE, choose [[Bounds]].

steps.title: Margin of error by hand
steps.suppose: we want the margin of error for 156 of 240 students, 92% confidence.
steps.observe: This is the amount added and subtracted. Subtract it from 0.65 for the lower bound and add it for the upper bound.
do: On a new row type `156/240` for $\hat p$.

steps.title: The whole interval in Desmos
steps.suppose: we want Desmos to build the 92% interval for 156 of 240.
steps.observe: Desmos shows the interval, the point estimate 0.65 and the standard error. Check that the numbers entered are 156 and 240 before reading the interval.
do: Press {plus}, then choose {inference}, then [[z-test for proportions]].
Enter 156 for successes and 240 for sample size, then press [[Create Test]].
Open the [[Confidence Interval]] tab and change the confidence level to 0.92.

steps.title: Work backwards: the margin of error
steps.suppose: we are given the 90% interval (0.42, 0.54) and want $\hat p$ and the margin of error.
steps.observe: The point estimate is always the midpoint of the interval and the margin of error is half its width.
do: On a new row type `(0.42+0.54)/2` for the midpoint.
On the next row type `(0.54-0.42)/2` for the half-width.

steps.title: Work backwards: the sample size
steps.suppose: we want $n$ for that interval, with $z^*=1.645$.
steps.observe: The result is 187.6. Round up to the next whole number so the margin of error is no larger than 0.06.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Defining the parameter without the population
traps.weak: $p$ is the proportion in the marching band.
traps.better: $p$ is the proportion of all teens in Ohio who are in a marching band.

traps.title: Naming the procedure
traps.better: A one-sample $z$ interval for a population proportion.

traps.title: Using $p$ in the standard error
traps.better: We do not know $p$, so the standard error uses $\hat p$: $\sqrt{\dfrac{0.239(0.761)}{380}}$.

traps.title: Writing the conclusion
traps.better: I am 92% confident that the proportion of all students in this district who support the new homework platform is between 0.596 and 0.704.

traps.title: Rounding the sample size down
traps.better: Always round up. $n=188$ makes the margin of error at most 0.06, and 187 would not.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion is (0.31, 0.43). What are the sample proportion and the margin of error?
why: The point estimate is the midpoint, not an endpoint, and 0.12 is the full width.
The midpoint is $(0.31+0.43)/2=0.37$ and the half-width is $(0.43-0.31)/2=0.06$.
0.12 is the width of the interval, which is two margins of error.
0.43 is the upper endpoint, not the point estimate.

questions.stem: A random sample of 200 people has $\hat p=0.35$. Which expression is the standard error used in a confidence interval?
why: 0.40 is not given anywhere. The standard error uses the sample proportion 0.35.
The whole fraction belongs under the square root, not just the numerator.
The square root should cover the whole fraction.

questions.stem: Which is the best conclusion for a 90% interval of (0.42, 0.54) for the proportion of registered voters in a county who support a tax increase?
opts: I am 90% confident that the proportion of all registered voters in the county who support the tax increase is between 0.42 and 0.54
There is a 90% chance the sample proportion is between 0.42 and 0.54
90% of voters support the tax increase
The proportion of voters is between 0.42 and 0.54
why: This gives the confidence level, the interval and the parameter in context.
The sample proportion is the midpoint of this interval and is known exactly.
The interval estimates a single proportion, not 90% of voters.
This leaves out the confidence level and the word confident.

questions.stem: Which value of $z^*$ is used for a 90% confidence interval?
why: 1.282 leaves 10% in one tail, not 10% in two tails.
90% in the middle leaves 5% in each tail, which gives $z^*=1.645$.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: A gym has 6,400 members. A researcher randomly selects 520 members and finds that 182 of them use the pool.
parts: (a) Name the procedure and define the parameter.
(b) Check the conditions for the procedure.
sample: (a) A one-sample $z$ interval for a population proportion. $p$ is the proportion of all members of the gym who use the pool.
(b) Random: the 520 members were randomly selected. 10%: 520 is less than 10% of 6,400, which is 640. Large counts: 182 successes and 338 failures, both at least 10.
(d) I am 90% confident that the proportion of all members of the gym who use the pool is between 0.316 and 0.384.
checklist: (a) Procedure named and parameter defined with population and variable
(b) Random, 10% (with 640) and large counts (182 and 338) checked
(c) Standard error built from $\hat p$, margin of error about 0.034
(d) Confidence level, interval and parameter in context
